result:
At the corner of my street, a small tree grows through a square of tired concrete. Nobody seems to know what kind it is. In spring, its leaves arrive as pale green commas, interrupting the long sentence of traffic. By August, they are dusty and stubborn, but still unmistakably alive.

Every morning, someone locks a bicycle to its protective railing. A delivery driver pauses beneath it to check an address. Once, after a storm, I watched a child gather fallen twigs and arrange them into a tiny bridge across a puddle. The tree offered no instructions, only materials and shade.

I like that it makes no attempt to be impressive. It does not bloom extravagantly or turn a famous color in autumn. Its branches lean toward the only reliable patch of sunlight, giving it a slightly lopsided posture. If trees could have handwriting, this one’s would be quick and uneven.

Last winter, a crew repaired the sidewalk around its roots. For several days, orange barriers surrounded the corner, and the tree looked oddly official, like a minor public figure awaiting a portrait. When the barriers disappeared, the new pavement curved around the trunk instead of insisting on a straight line.

That small curve pleases me. Cities often ask living things to behave like furniture: stay put, take up less room, cause no trouble. Yet here, for once, the hard surface made an adjustment. I walk past without ceremony, grateful for a reminder that accommodation can be built into ordinary ground.
